takeaway: Flame centralizes serverless function-cache decisions across a cluster, separating hotspot and best-effort caches to reduce cold starts and memory waste under skewed demand.
background: Serverless platforms keep finished function instances warm to avoid container cold starts, but those instances consume memory. Existing controllers commonly decide locally at each server.
villain: With skewed request distributions, local controllers can colocate hot functions while redundantly retaining cold ones because no controller sees cluster-wide load and cache reuse.
approach: Flame adds a global CacheManager and a Cachelet on every OpenFaaS server. The manager detects hot functions with an exponentially decayed score and places them to minimize aggregate hotspot pressure; each Cachelet protects hot instances, keeps other instances in evictable temporary space, and reclaims overprovisioned hot instances. The design depends on periodically synchronized cluster state and a responsive central controller, while the current scheduler models only memory capacity.
impact: The authors argue that cluster-wide cache control can maintain warm invocations with substantially less memory than local policies for the evaluated serverless traces.

evaluation.overview: An OpenFaaS prototype was exercised on an eight-server cluster with eight sampled Azure trace workloads mapped to 384 functions from ServerlessBench and FunctionBench; a simulator explored parameters and larger scales.
evaluation.implemented: About 4,000 lines of Go integrated a CacheManager, per-server Cachelets, and keep-alive control into OpenFaaS; separate Java test and simulation code supported trace-driven experiments.
evaluation.setting: Eight 32-core Intel Xeon Silver 4215 servers, each with 256 GB RAM and 10 Gb/s Ethernet, ran Ubuntu 16.04; each one-week workload contained 384 functions sampled from Azure traces, whose arrivals drove matched benchmark functions.

results.text: Under consistent-hashing dispatch across eight traces, the authors report that Flame used 36% less cache memory on average than FaasCache and 33% less than CH-RLU.
In the eight-server breakdown, the authors report a 0.86% cold-start ratio and 0.02% request-drop ratio for Flame, versus 1.83% and 0.77% for FaasCache.

limitations: The measured prototype used an eight-server testbed and benchmark functions driven by sampled Azure arrivals rather than Azure function code. Scheduling currently considers only memory, protected-space usage is uncapped in extreme cases, and the centralized controller may need partitioning at very large scale.
phd_group_signal: The work reflects a full-system methodology: diagnose trace skew, co-design global and per-node policies, implement them in OpenFaaS, and test both on hardware and by simulation.

claims.text: Flame combines a global CacheManager with per-server Cachelets, hotspot-aware placement, protected and temporary cache spaces, and local adaptive reclamation.
CacheManager and Cachelets synchronize state every five seconds, current placement considers only memory, and protected cache space has no capacity threshold.
The authors warn that a centralized CacheManager may face scalability problems in extremely large clusters and evaluate workload partitioning as a mitigation.

The prototype contains about 4,000 lines of Go and was evaluated on eight 32-core Xeon Silver 4215 servers with 256 GB RAM and 10 Gb/s networking, using eight one-week traces of 384 sampled Azure functions mapped to benchmark functions.
